extracted.intended_audience: Attorneys and practitioners who practice before the USPTO (especially trademark practitioners), counsel in USPTO OED disciplinary matters, and law firm managers overseeing trademark filing procedures
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria used by the USPTO Tribunal to assess alleged violations of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct in disciplinary proceedings (here, focused on improperly executed trademark signatures). Includes procedural rules, elements of proof, substantive ethical duties, and sanctioning factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — clear and convincing evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving any alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence, and the respondent bears the burden of proving any affirmative defenses by clear and convincing evidence. "Clear and convincing" requires evidence of such weight that it produces a firm belief or conviction, without hesitancy, or proves the facts to be 'highly probable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intermediate standard between 'beyond a reasonable doubt' and 'preponderance of the evidence'; evidence must produce an 'abiding conviction' or be 'highly probable.' (Cites Jimenez v. DaimlerChrysler, Colorado v. New Mexico.) Use this standard when weighing disputed factual assertions in OED matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO authority and disciplinary procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO has exclusive authority to establish qualifications for practicing before it and to suspend or exclude practitioners; disciplinary proceedings are governed by 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32 and 37 C.F.R. part 11, and are conducted with notice and opportunity for hearing under the Administrative Procedure Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural requirements include notice, opportunity for hearing, impartial hearing officer, record, post-hearing briefs, and right to appeal to the USPTO Director. Procedural compliance (timeliness, hearing rights, etc.) is part of the evaluative framework for OED cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of diligence — 37 C.F.R. § 11.103
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must act with reasonable diligence in representing clients; failure to pay attention to how delegated tasks (e.g., obtaining client signatures) are being performed can violate § 11.103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delegating important tasks is permitted only if the attorney reasonably ensures they are done in compliance with law and rules. A lack of any effort to determine how assistants obtain signatures (e.g., unquestioning reliance on firm workflow) can be negligent and breach § 11.103. Prior decisions (Khalsa, Bethell, Pasquine) illustrate violations where attorneys failed to verify signature procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisory responsibility regarding non-practitioner assistants — 37 C.F.R. § 11.503
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner who employs, retains, or associates with non-practitioner assistants must make reasonable efforts to ensure the assistants’ conduct is compatible with the practitioner’s professional obligations. If the practitioner is a partner, has comparable managerial authority, or has direct supervisory authority and knows of assistant misconduct, the practitioner is responsible if they fail to take reasonable remedial action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability under § 11.503 hinges on whether the attorney had direct supervisory or managerial authority. Junior associates without supervisory authority are less likely to be held responsible under § 11.503. Evaluate the attorney’s role, firm structure, and actual supervisory control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark signature requirements — 37 C.F.R. § 2.193 and TMEP § 611.01(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: All correspondence requiring a signature must bear a handwritten or electronic signature personally entered by the named signatory. Another person (paralegal, legal assistant, or secretary) may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner or other authorized signatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance with § 2.193 and TMEP guidance is mandatory. When assessing filings, confirm whether the signature was personally entered by the listed signatory. Noncompliance (signatures entered by others) is a rule violation and relevant to claims of negligence or prejudicial conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: TEAS electronic signature methods (DIRECT vs ESIGN-ON)
rubrics_metrics.description: TEAS permits electronic signatures entered by typing between two forward slashes. The DIRECT method requires the TEAS user preparing the document to type the signature himself; ESIGN-ON sends a link to an outside email address allowing the third party to enter the signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish DIRECT-signed documents (indicates the preparer typed the signature) from ESIGN-ON (link sent for third-party signature). Use XML/TEAS metadata and IP address information to determine how a signature was entered; DIRECT signatures submitted from remote IPs (e.g., India) can indicate improper practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice — 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes conduct that impedes or subverts dispute resolution or frustrates the fair balance of interests essential to proceedings; conduct that degrades the integrity of the registration system or undermines public confidence can be prejudicial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly allowing improperly signed filings into the USPTO trademark register — even if unintentional and without client harm — can be prejudicial because it undermines the integrity and public confidence in the system. Use this standard when misconduct affects systemic reliability rather than only individual clients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation — 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibits conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation. Generally requires an intent to deceive; negligent or mistaken misrepresentations, without intent, typically do not violate § 11.804(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing a § 11.804(c) violation requires evidence of subjective intent to deceive or conscious dishonesty. Prior decisions show that sincere but mistaken beliefs or mere negligence are insufficient to prove § 11.804(c) violations; look for evidence of knowing falsity or deceptive intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client communication obligations — 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) and (b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter and explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess timeliness and reasonableness of communications given what the attorney knew and when. Delayed notification may be reasonable if the attorney lacked verifiable information or was following firm management’s guidance, but unexplained prolonged silence when the attorney had knowledge is problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor to the tribunal (USPTO) — 37 C.F.R. § 11.303 and § 11.1
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to a tribunal, fail to correct a false statement previously made, or omit to inform a tribunal of material facts in ex parte proceedings. The Office is considered a 'tribunal' for purposes of § 11.303.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duty of candor requires disclosure or remedial measures if practitioner knows evidence offered is false or a person intends fraudulent conduct related to a proceeding. In ex parte matters, material facts known to the practitioner must be disclosed regardless of adversarial impact. Evaluate whether the practitioner had 'actual knowledge' before requiring disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge standard for 'knowingly' and 'known' (37 C.F.R. § 11.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The words 'knowingly,' 'known,' or 'knows' require actual knowledge of the fact in question; 'knowledge' is defined as conscious awareness of the nature or attendant circumstances of the conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determinations under §§ that use 'knowingly' depend on actual, subjective knowledge. Absent evidence of actual knowledge, a practitioner may not be found to have 'knowingly' violated duties. Willful blindness requires proof; mere suspicion or negligence does not equal knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions determination framework — 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) and ABA Standards
rubrics_metrics.description: When imposing sanctions the Tribunal must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the conduct was intentional, knowing, or negligent; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury; and (4) aggravating or mitigating factors. The Tribunal often looks to the ABA Standards for guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the four-factor framework and weigh aggravating factors (e.g., pattern of misconduct) against mitigating factors (e.g., absence of dishonest motive, remediation, clean disciplinary history, remorse). Use ABA Standards sections (e.g., § 9.22, § 9.32) for analogues when selecting appropriate sanction (public reprimand, suspension, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negligence definition and culpability
rubrics_metrics.description: Negligence is defined as the failure to take reasonable care; negligent misconduct is treated differently than knowing or intentional misconduct in sanctioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negligent conduct can warrant discipline but typically less severe sanctions than intentional or fraudulent conduct. Evidence that attorney failed to exercise reasonable care (e.g., never checked how signatures were obtained) supports finding of negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial measures and mitigation (client ratification and voluntary amendments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing voluntary amendments to ratify client signatures, notifying affected clients, and changing practice (e.g., personally handling filings) are remedial steps that can mitigate discipline and satisfy duties of candor/rectification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful remedial actions (contacting clients, filing ratifications where possible, altering firm procedures) are mitigating factors. Note: some remedial filings may be questioned by USPTO, but the effort evidences mitigation and good-faith remediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for final decision, appeal, and publication of discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial decisions become final absent appeal to the USPTO Director within specified time (e.g., 14 days). Sanctions such as public reprimands are published in the USPTO Official Gazette and disciplinary decisions are posted in OED reading materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include appeal timelines and publication obligations when advising practitioners about the practical consequences of a disciplinary order and post-decision rights; courts of review and correction (e.g., nunc pro tunc corrections) are available for scrivener errors.
